title: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: Network Logon Script
shortTitle: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: Network Logon Script
summary: Network logon scripts are command files stored centrally, usually on a domain controller, that Active Directory or a Group Policy Object assigns so they execute on a workstation each time an assigned user signs in. They run with the privileges of the user they are attached to, not as the system, so an adversary needs only the ability to edit a script or add one to a user object or policy rather than administrative control of every endpoint. The value to an intruder is scale: one edited file can execute on every machine in a site, a department, or the whole domain at the next logon, making it a durable persistence and privilege position that survives reimaging of individual hosts. Detection rests on change control rather than unusual endpoint behaviour. Relevant artefacts include the script files under the Netlogon share, Group Policy settings that name them, directory service change events on the user or policy object, and the interpreter process that starts during logon on each client, such as a command shell or scripting host reading a script from a network path. Legitimate scripts change during planned maintenance windows and are reviewed, so unexplained edits or new script paths outside that process are the clear signal.

beginner.definition: A network logon script is a small file of commands kept on a server. The domain tells a computer to run that file each time a chosen user signs in. It is a simple way for an administrator to set up many machines at once.
beginner.whyItMatters: These scripts run by design, so nobody is surprised when one starts. A single changed script can run on hundreds of computers the next morning. It runs with the user's own permissions, so an attacker can use it without stealing an administrator password. Many organisations never review the contents after the first setup.
howItWorks: An administrator writes a command file and stores it in a shared folder on a server.
The script is linked to a user account or to a policy that covers a group of computers.
When an assigned user signs in, the client fetches the script over the network and runs it.
An attacker with rights to edit the file or the policy adds their own commands to it.
The user signs in as normal and the extra commands run quietly in the background.
A policy refresh can also push the change out to many machines without any reboot.
beginner.example: Think of a chain of shops with a morning checklist sent from head office. It says to unlock the doors, switch on the lights and start the tills. Staff follow it every day without questioning it. If somebody slips one extra line into the master checklist, every shop opens the back gate as well. The staff are only doing what the official list says.
takeaways: Network logon scripts are a central file that runs on many machines at sign-in.
Treat the script share and the policies that name scripts as high value code.
Review who can change these files, and alert on edits made outside a change window.

objectives: Define a network logon script and explain how Active Directory or Group Policy delivers it.
Explain why editing one script can affect many hosts at the next user logon.
Describe the privileges a network logon script runs with and what that means for an attacker.
List the artefacts, such as script files and policy changes, that a defender can review.
Recommend change control and monitoring for centrally stored logon scripts.
